item.title: Restoring peace to the hills. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The recurring clashes and exchanges of gunfire between rival armed groups in Sajek potentially signal a resurgence of instability in the Chittagong Hill Tracts (CHT) that must not be taken lightly.
We should not be tolerating territorial rivalries erupting into open gunbattles as innocent local residents are forced to live in constant terror. This is equally true for tourism, local economies, and public safety which are repeatedly held hostage.
Such lawlessness cannot be treated as an inevitable feature of the region; bringing lasting peace, security, and the rule of law to the hills must become an immediate, non-negotiable priority.
For far too long, armed factions in the CHT have continued to operate, waging turf wars for political dominance. All the while, it has been civilian populations that have been affected.
Recent blockades, attacks on tourist convoys, and armed standoffs not only imperil local livelihoods but also directly challenge state authority. Law enforcement and security personnel stating that they struggle to access remote clash sites while communities are caught in the crossfire is simply not enough of a reason.
Peace in the CHT cannot be sustained through temporary ceasefires or passive monitoring from a distance. While political dialogue, genuine socio-economic development, and the full implementation of structural commitments remain vital for long-term reconciliation, the immediate priority must also be to ensure the safety and security of those who call the region home.
The people of the Chittagong Hill Tracts deserve safety, dignity, and economic progress, not perpetual warfare. It is time for the government to commit to the region, first by restoring peace.

item.title: Our education must move beyond grades. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We understand the immediate concern that comes from the drastic decline in this year’s Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examination pass rate.
Dropping by 6.71% down to 52.12%, alongside hundreds of thousands of failures, and institutions recording zero pass rates will inevitably trigger panicked headlines across the country. This newspaper has been no different.
On the surface, such a significant drop cannot simply be brushed aside as an administrative quirk. It is only natural to wonder what has happened for the number of students securing a GPA-5 to fall from 145,911 in 2024 to 40,084 in 2026 -- a drop of more than 72%.
Yet, reacting with reflexive hand-wringing or frantic attempts to massage the numbers misses the deeper, more vital reality.
For decades, our education system has prioritized pass rates and inflated GPA-5 tallies, fostering a culture of rote memorization, coaching-centre dependency, and superficial evaluation that has left our students fundamentally unequipped for the real world.
When students emerge from 12 years of schooling unable to analyze, adapt, or compete in a modernizing global economy, chasing a GPA-5 becomes a hollow and deceptive pursuit.
The state, educators, and parents must stop treating board exams as a bureaucratic obstacle course and start interrogating the structural "whys" behind our chronic learning deficits -- including acute teacher shortages, outdated curricula, and an assessment system that penalizes analytical thought.
Tackling our education crisis requires the government to look beyond annual statistical fluctuations. We need an overhaul of our education culture, one that pivots away from rote memorization toward competency-based education.
A 52% pass rate is a harsh wake-up call, but it should not be treated as a disaster to be masked by artificial grading leniency. Instead, it must serve as the catalyst to dismantle prioritizing grades over all.
It is time to stop chasing cosmetic metrics and finally invest in our youth's future by having an education system that builds capable, well-rounded citizens equipped to excel in life.

item.title: The next frontier of digital financial inclusion. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A small printed QR code now prominently sits near the counter of almost every shop and market stall across Dhaka. Bangla QR, Bangladesh Bank’s interoperable payment system, is one of the most significant pieces of financial infrastructure that the country has built in years.
Any customer, irrespective of which bank or mobile financial service they are using, can pay any merchant by scanning just one QR code. It is meant to finally tie together a payment ecosystem that has long operated in silos, and carries real potential to catalyze the next major shift in how this country manages its money.
Government policies have already produced measurable results. According to Bangladesh Bank and the World Bank, more than 53% of the population now holds a bank account, while the number of registered mobile financial service accounts had reached 239.3 million by January 2026.
No frill accounts, which include low-income, student, and “street urchin” banking, now number 36,648,119, holding deposits of Tk90,101.37 million, according to Bangladesh Bank’s Financial Inclusion Report (April-June 2026).
However, the gap becomes clear if you compare these data with regional peers. Among Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, India, Pakistan, and Nepal, account ownership ranges from Sri Lanka’s 89% down to Pakistan’s 21%, with India at 78% and Nepal at 54%.
But these two extreme ends of the spectrum are not necessarily the best benchmarks. Sri Lanka has the highest per capita income and literacy rate among all nations in the region, while Nepal has an economy that relies on remittance and tourism rather than its domestic financial depth.
India and Pakistan offer the fairer comparison since they share similar income levels and developing economies with sizeable informal sectors and broadly similar macroeconomic pressures.
Among these two, India has shown how deliberately account ownership can be engineered through policy. In 2014, the country launched “Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana,” a national program built around a single objective: A formal bank account for every household.
The World Bank has attributed much of India’s sharp rise in account ownership between 2014 and 2017 directly to that program, which used official identification to draw previously unbanked citizens into the formal system.
This was followed by the UPI, India’s interoperable payments infrastructure, which brought together a landscape that had been as fragmented as Bangladesh’s remains today.
Private companies like ‘Paytm’ and ‘PhonePe’ took advantage of this and today, the results can be seen on the ground level where even street vendors all across Indian cities accept digital payment with no issues.
Bangladesh has built something close to UPI with its Bangla QR. With this, an everyday barrier to using formal financial channels has been removed. Additionally, through the National Payment Switch Bangladesh (NPSB), interoperability now runs in both directions; funds move from MFS to bank and bank to MFS with the same ease as MFS-to-MFS or bank-to-bank transfers.
The problem now is that the population is yet to fully comprehend how to plan, save, or invest their money. There has been rapid growth in MFS penetration in the country. But the majority of these users who know how to send or receive money, still do not understand basic concepts such as how micro-insurance functions or why a mutual fund or digital DPS might serve their long-term interest better than idle cash.
This gap leads us back to the lack of financial literacy among people in this country. According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics, we have a general literacy rate of 77.9%. However, our financial literacy stands at only 28% which means more than 70% of the population lacks the fundamental understanding of basic financial concepts.
There is no alternative to financial literacy if we want people to be able to manage their money well and make decisions suited to their circumstances. No platform or policy can make those choices on a person’s behalf.
It’s imperative to integrate financial literacy into the educational curriculum so that people grow up learning about financial concepts that will later help them manage their finances in life.
We also need more community-based campaigns and more programs on gender inclusive financial literacy. The government, financial institutions, and private sector must all come forward with easy and convenient financial tools so that it’s more accessible for people regardless of income, demographic, or gender.
The government has set its sights on a trillion-dollar economy by 2034, and it is hard to see how that can be achieved with a financial system that marginalizes half of its adult population.
An economy grows through the circulation of capital, and the capital circulates most effectively when people can save, borrow, invest, and transact through proper channels rather than informal channels.
A trillion-dollar economy needs savers and investors as much as it needs payers and, on that count, we still have a long way to go.
Syed Javed Noor is the AMD & Head of Business of IDLC Finance PLC.

item.title: Getting another chance to graduate right. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh’s three-year extension before graduating from the least developed country (LDC) category is welcome news, but it should also serve as a serious reminder of the work that remains.
The deadline has moved to November 2029, which means the country can use this additional time to prepare for a transition that will bring greater competition and fewer trade advantages.
Bangladesh has met the UN’s graduation criteria, but meeting the indicators does not mean the economy is ready to withstand the loss of preferential market access and other benefits. Our export sector, particularly the ready-made garment industry, remains heavily dependent on these advantages.
Without stronger trade arrangements and more competitive industries, exporters could face higher costs and lose ground to rivals.
The next three years must therefore be treated as a period of focused reform, and not a reason to put difficult decisions on hold. Strengthening the banking sector, addressing non-performing loans, widening the tax base, and improving revenue collection are essential.
Equally important is reducing the cost of doing business through reliable energy, better infrastructure, efficient ports, and simpler regulations. Long-promised reforms must move beyond policy documents and produce measurable results.
We must also move away from our dependence on a narrow range of exports. Supporting sectors such as pharmaceuticals, leather, light engineering, and other promising industries can create new sources of foreign earnings and employment.
At the same time, trade negotiations must be pursued with urgency -- particularly with major markets such as the European Union.
We must acknowledge that this extension is an opportunity, not a reprieve from responsibility. Government agencies, businesses, and policymakers must work towards clear targets, timelines, and accountability.
If the next three years are spent by strategically addressing weaknesses and building competitiveness, our upcoming graduation can become a milestone of genuine economic strength.
If we fail to do so, however, we will simply find the nation faces the same challenges later, with even less room to prepare.

item.title: Wake up, Bangladesh. We need sports science. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We often see a common scenario, from the remote areas of our country to the international level. The picture is almost the same everywhere.
Let me explain.
Imagine a football match. Our striker is inside the opponent’s penalty box. He skillfully dribbles past a defender and is just about to take a shot at goal. If he takes that shot properly, it is a goal.
But at that very moment, he misses the target. Maybe his foot timing is wrong, or he takes a weak shot. Some of us feel disappointed, some criticize him, and some think there will be another opportunity.
But even when another opportunity comes, the same thing keeps happening again and again.
This is a normal scenario for us. The tournaments organized by FIFA are proof of that. From age-group teams to the senior national team, we have the same situation and almost the same results.
More or less, the same thing happens in other sports as well. Once in a while, we might win a medal at some international event, but even that is akin to a miracle.
We have no Olympic medals. We have no significant position in international football. Although cricket has progressed, we still have not won a major international tournament trophy.
No matter how much we make sports compulsory at the primary, secondary, and college levels, we still do not know what we actually need to do.
Have you ever thought about what happens after that dribble past the defender? What is the level of your physical strength at that moment? How much stamina do you have left? What is your mental state when you are about to take that exact shot?
Can your brain think properly under high-intensity conditions? Are your muscles able to support the skills you have learned, and is your brain providing the right support to execute those skills? What is your work capacity?
We don’t know these things. We really don’t.
Let me give you another example.
You are a 100-metre sprinter. Your coach tells you that your start is not good enough and tries to improve it. He keeps teaching you and correcting your technique again and again. That’s good. But why is your start not good in the first place?
Is there a problem with your gait? Did you once suffer an ankle sprain that you never fully recovered from?
Even if you did recover, do you know how to return to training, what level of capacity you should return with, or how long you can sustain that capacity?
You don’t know.
Meanwhile, you keep trying to fix your poor start without understanding the actual reason behind it.
Athletes in developed countries do not win medals for no reason. They win because of the process behind their performance. They win because of the preparation that goes into winning.
They do not win medals simply because they start a race and run all the way to the finish line. They win because of the entire process, from the very first footstep at the beginning of their sporting journey to the moment they finally stand on the champions’ podium.
They win because of science. Sports science.
In Bangladesh, Sports science is still a profession that many people hesitate to openly identify as their occupation when someone asks them what they do for a living.
I am waiting for that day when a 14- or 15-year-old boy who dreams of representing his country will not simply be pushed into a sport without proper evaluation.
Instead, before his body is introduced to the demands of that sport, he will undergo a proper assessment, and science will be integrated into his physical and mental development according to a structured process.
But for this to happen, we need more than just coaches.
When it comes to the development of sports in our country, appointing district coaches and assistant coaches is not where the responsibility ends. A coach alone cannot address every aspect of an athlete’s development. We need a proper support system built around our athletes.
Appoint sports scientists in every district. Appoint sports psychologists. Appoint qualified trainers and strength and conditioning professionals. Build a system where coaches, sports scientists, psychologists, and trainers work together to evaluate athletes, monitor their progress, prevent injuries, support rehabilitation, and improve performance through a scientific approach.
If we continue to ignore these essential aspects of athlete development, our sports will remain at the bottom and may sink even further.
We cannot expect different results while continuing to follow the same approach. We cannot keep expecting miracles and call them a development strategy.
Results and medals do not come in a single day. They require time, planning, evaluation, professional expertise, and a scientific approach.
Some of us have been raising our voices for so long, yet the reality remains almost the same. How much longer do we have to keep shouting before someone from the authorities finally listens?
How much longer must we wait before sports in Bangladesh are treated as a science, a profession, and a system that deserves proper investment?
Miftab Uddin is a sports teacher at Scholastica school.

item.title: Ridding society of regressive norms. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The death of 24-year-old Zumratun Nesa Barsha, reportedly following repeated abuse over dowry demands, is not only an unacceptable tragedy itself, but is a devastating reminder that deeply entrenched social practices continue to destroy women's lives in Bangladesh.
Reports indicate that Barsha had been facing abuse over dowry demands, and her husband has since been arrested in connection with her death. But while the circumstances of her death remain murky and must be established through a proper investigation, this incident demands that we confront a much wider problem.
This is also an opportunity to resume dialogue on societal norms that must be stopped.
Dowry is not the only regressive practice that continues to undermine women's dignity and safety: Child marriage, forced marriages, restrictions on women's education and mobility, and the expectation that women must endure abuse to preserve family honour are all rooted in outdated attitudes that have no place in a modern society. They perpetuate the idea that women have fewer rights, less autonomy, and less value than men.
Bangladesh has laws prohibiting dowry and child marriage, but legislation alone cannot dismantle practices that continue to enjoy social acceptance in many communities. Families must stop treating these customs as inevitable, while communities must actively challenge those who defend or encourage them. We must also move away from the culture of silence that pressures women to tolerate abuse rather than seek help.
Law enforcement agencies must start taking complaints seriously, investigating allegations promptly, and ensuring perpetrators are brought to justice. Women facing abuse must have access to legal protection and safe places to turn to, without being pressured to preserve marriages at the expense of their safety.
It is high time we not only moved away from, but actively denounced these retrograde practices. A society cannot claim to be progressing while continuing to tolerate customs that strip women of their dignity, independence and, sometimes, their lives.
